turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Wednesday, the twenty-sixth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three to tease. Washington declares an economic D-Day on Iran… and the oil price falls.
[curious] Falls? On a war-on-the-oil-money story? Okay, I need that one.
Two. Gold at a three-month high, a new Fed chair's first Jackson Hole on Friday, and one chip company's earnings the whole market is holding its breath for.
[warmly] And three — my favourite — the headphone hobby, where a graph and a pair of ears have been at war for twenty years.
And a two-hundred-dollar Sennheiser keeps winning it. We'll get there.
[chuckles] We always get there. Start me with the D-Day.

So. The Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, writes an op-ed calling Monday's sanctions package — and I'm quoting — an economic D-Day, the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary.
That's… a lot of words.

It is a lot of words. On the day, Treasury names close to sixty firms, people and vessels — several of them Chinese. Iran's security chief threatens to shut the Strait of Hormuz. Not a single drop of oil, he says.
[skeptical] And Hormuz is — what, a fifth of the world's seaborne crude? That threat should move the barrel ten dollars.
It moved it down. Brent fell almost four per cent, to about eighty-eight dollars and change.
[gasps] Down. Why down?

Because traders read the theatre. The branding was for the audience; the barrel is for people who've learned to discount a Hormuz headline. And the Washington Post noticed the small print — Bessent delayed the toughest measures. Built in a grace period. He even admitted hitting everything at once could blow up the global financial system.
So the declaration is the deterrent, and the delay is the actual policy.
[wry] You've read the desk.
[laughs] I read one line of the desk. What's Beijing say?

That sanctions aren't the solution, and China–Iran cooperation shouldn't be disrupted. Which matters, because there's a Trump–Xi summit set for the twenty-fourth of September. You can't enforce hard against Chinese firms three weeks before that without wrecking it.
[thoughtful] So the leverage that's supposed to squeeze Tehran is the same leverage that protects it. That's the whole gap, isn't it — the announcement, and then the stubborner fact underneath.
That's the spine of the whole issue, actually. Facts are stubborn things — it's our quote today, John Adams, seventeen-seventy. He said it to a jury he needed to cool.
[warmly] Adams to a jury. I like that. Okay — money block. Give me the markets.
One force, four instruments. The dollar is soft, hike odds are fading, and the Treasury is quietly funding its own long bond through buybacks.
Translate the bond bit for me.

The thirty-year yield spiked to five point three three per cent last week — a nineteen-year high. Then the Treasury signalled it would buy back its own debt, and the yield eased to about five and a quarter.
[amused] The issuer rescues its own market.

And that soft-dollar, lower-real-rate mix lifts two things at once. Gold to a three-month high — about four thousand, six hundred and thirty-nine dollars. And bitcoin up roughly twenty-eight per cent on the month, into the low eighty-thousands.
[curious] And the dollar and the yen?
The dollar index slid below ninety-nine, down two and a half per cent on the month. The yen's weak — about a hundred and fifty-nine to the dollar. The Singapore dollar's firm, near one-twenty-seven.
[curious] Note you said three-month high on gold. Not record.
[deadpan] Not a record. We corrected ourselves on that. It's a three-month high; the January peak was higher. The number matters.
Good. And Friday?
Friday is Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole as Fed chair. The market has basically pre-declared it a non-event — about seven in ten managers expect a neutral tone.
Which is exactly why it's dangerous.
Right. If everyone's priced neutral, the surprise is a hawk. And Warsh is a career hawk, with three dissents behind him for a hike, not a cut. This is explanation, by the way — not advice.
Always. And the thing everyone's actually waiting for is tonight.

Nvidia. Reports after the US close — which is after we go to bed here, so we're previewing, not printing. The guide is ninety-one billion dollars in a quarter. Data centre is more than ninety-two per cent of the company.
One number, the whole trade.

One number. And the sceptic's line is sharp — it's about debt, not demand. One firm borrowing at nine per cent to earn under one. An MIT survey found ninety-five per cent of enterprise A-I pilots showed no measurable profit.
[exhales] Ninety-five per cent. Okay. Bring it home to Singapore.
Two things. The Foreign Ministry called Israel's E-one settlement plan illegal under international law — a firm word, and, unlike some European partners, no material lever behind it.
A word without a sanction.
A word without a sanction. And the cradle. The National Day Rally leg this week doubles childcare leave and ties it to family size — eight days for one child, twelve for three or more.
But the birth rate.

But the birth rate keeps sliding, and the forums are doing the arithmetic: cash can't fix housing cost, career cost, the load. The state has spent the better part of seventy thousand dollars a child, and the number won't move.
[thoughtful] Another declaration, another stubborn fact. The policy says have babies; the number says not yet.
Stay on that theme — it runs through tech, too. A Chinese lab, Z-A-I, built a model so good at finding software holes it's holding its own weights back. The window to release closes around Friday.
A vendor withholding open weights because they're too good. That's a new one.

And Washington's moving on the rent-a-G-P-U loophole — firms renting Nvidia chips offshore to dodge export controls. One rented two thousand three hundred of them through Indonesia; another secured fifteen thousand through Japan.
[amused] Meanwhile, in my tower — anything good for the home lab?
Actually yes. The most-used local engine now ships agent tools built in. Your own model can read, write and run files, no server, no glue code.
On a card I already own?
On a card you already own — if you can afford the card. A five-thousand-nine-oh costs about four thousand seven hundred dollars on the street now. More than double list.
[scoffs] So the software's free and the hardware's the tax. Classic.
Classic. And on The Kit — Garmin's flagship went official. The fēnix nine. From about a thousand US dollars; the Pro adds a titanium case and satellite messaging from the wrist.
[skeptical] A thousand dollars. What do the owners say?
Impressive, but incremental. They're calling it a half-step over last year. Reviewers were still gagged at launch, so that's the spec sheet, not the wrist.
[warmly] One thing I did like this week — the Sennheiser earbud you can re-battery yourself. Screwdriver in the box.
Three hundred dollars, and a real answer to disposable buds. The genuine upgrades this week were the ones that fixed a known failure, not the ones that added a nit or a gigabyte.
Give me one buy-once thing before the rabbit hole.
The Atelier did kitchen knives. And the lesson is beautiful: a knife is three decisions — steel, hardness, geometry. None of them is the badge.
[curious] Teach me one number.

Twenty-five to a hundred dollars is the real jump in cutting feel. A hundred to three hundred buys much less than you think. And a sharp forty-nine-dollar Victorinox out-cuts a neglected four-hundred-dollar knife every time.
And who really makes the fancy ones?

That's the fun part. The luxury Japanese brand a lot of people buy — Miyabi — is owned by a German company and made in a Japanese town called Seki. And the grail names in the forums, like Shigefusa, are half romance. Even the fans admit it.
[laughs] So the whole luxury ladder is… learn to sharpen.
Learn to sharpen. And you don't need eight knives. A chef's knife, a small one, a bread knife. That's the kitchen.
[thoughtful] And carbon steel — does it rust here?

In Singapore's humidity, fast. So a first-timer buys stainless, unless he wants the wipe-it-dry-every-time ritual. Either way, the whetstone is the thing that makes it buy-once — not the maker's name.
[warmly] I love this desk. Okay. It's time.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] Headphones, Claire. The hobby where you buy a pair of ears a better recording.
That's the gateway, honestly. A track you've heard a thousand times, and suddenly there's a cymbal decaying in a room, a breath before the vocal. You never heard that before.
And then you're gone.
Then you're gone. And it's a real world — the main forum has around one and a half million members. The whole thing fits on a desk; no room to treat, no neighbours to annoy.
So what's the twenty-year war?
Measurement versus ears. One camp ranks gear by lab numbers — if it measures transparent, it is transparent. The other says the ear hears what the graph misses.
[curious] And the gear? Give me the ladder — I want the top.

In-ears run from about a hundred and fifty dollars — the current darling — up to grail pairs near three thousand seven hundred. And you can get them moulded to your own ear; there's a Singapore maker, Jomo Audio, that builds a flagship to order.
And over-ears?
The eternal recommendation is a two-hundred-dollar Sennheiser. Above it, a thousand-seven-hundred-dollar one, then Focal, then the planar grail — the HIFIMAN Susvara, six thousand dollars.
[excited] And there's a catch with that one, isn't there. I can feel it.

[amused] There's always a catch. The Susvara is the hardest-to-drive headphone made — eighty-three decibels per milliwatt. The community insists it wants a speaker amplifier, not a headphone one, to come alive.
So you buy the six-thousand-dollar headphone and then you buy an amplifier to make it work.

And that's before the electrostatic summit, where the top setup costs as much as a car. The one real bit of news this year is a subtraction — a beloved custom maker, Empire Ears, closed its doors in February.
[gasps] Closed? A summit-fi name?
A decade in, and gone. Called a gut-punch to the hobby — a sign that four-figure wired earpieces face a shrinking, wireless-first world. Even the grail tier is a hard business to run.
[laughs] Okay, that's absurd. Where's the exit?

The exit is early, and this is the honest part. Digital converters hit transparency for about a hundred dollars. Headphones hit diminishing returns around three to five hundred. Cables and tweaks are mostly snake oil — across seventeen blind tests, fourteen found no difference.
And the community admits it.
The community admits it. Their own conscience is that two-hundred-dollar Sennheiser embarrassing gear ten times its price. Chase the music, not the graph.
[warmly] If you're in Singapore, where do you go?
Adelphi mall — Jaben, the famous headphone shop. And CanJam every May, the one weekend to hear the car-priced stuff back to back.
[thoughtful] I could lose a whole Saturday there. And a whole salary.
Speaking of buying the finish and not the function — a lovely watch story. Minase, an Akita workshop, dropped its price by two-thirds.
How?

By putting a Japanese movement in it instead of a Swiss one. Two thousand, one hundred and fifty dollars. And the sceptic's line is the kind one: you're paying for the mirror polish, not the mechanics, and the brand says so out loud.
[warmly] Honesty as a feature. What else is out?
A Seoul group, NCT one-two-seven, turned ten and swept iTunes overnight — number one in more than ten markets by the next morning.
A hit?
[deadpan] A sweep. Not the same thing. A day-one fandom spike measures how fast a devoted base buys, not how long a record lasts. Watch the first-week numbers.
And that Djokovic film?
Still waiting on the critics. Premiered last week, and there's no aggregate score yet — a handful of raves, one big reservation. We're not calling it acclaimed until the number exists.
Fair. Family desk — the one you flagged.
Australia banned under-sixteens from social media. The platforms removed nearly five million accounts. And more than eight in ten under-sixteens are still on it.
[exhales] The gate leaks.

The gate leaks. And a big study links early, heavy use to earlier experimenting with alcohol and cannabis — but it's an association, not a sentence. A leading psychologist says the panic is mostly grounded in fiction.
So what does a parent of a twelve-year-old actually do?
Protect sleep. Phone charging outside the bedroom. The school day's phone-free now anyway. Guardrails beat bans. General guidance — not medical advice.
And my favourite reality check — the weighted vests.
[wry] Your rucking phase is over. A twelve-month trial: the weighted vest did not save the hip during weight loss, and it lost to plain lifting for muscle.
[laughs] Don't. I bought the vest.
Keep it for the walk. Just don't skip the barbell. That's the finding in a sentence.
[warmly] Okay. Take us out slow. The Long Read.
This one's quiet, and it's from Japan. As Tokyo and Beijing hit their coldest point in a decade… young Japanese women are queuing for the most Chinese dish to arrive in a generation.
What's the dish?
Malatang. A build-your-own Sichuan soup — you pick the ingredients off a wall, by weight, and they come back in a numbing chilli broth.
[curious] And the numbers are real?

Eleven specialty stores in twenty-twenty-two. Ninety-three new ones in the first nine months of twenty-twenty-five. One Chinese chain alone runs sixty-two shops in Japan now. Eight or nine in ten customers are women in their teens and twenties.
[thoughtful] While the two governments freeze each other out.

While the governments freeze. China banned Japanese seafood, cancelled exchanges. And a Chinese soup chain opens a Japanese outlet nearly every month. The ministry and the market are describing two different countries.
And it came the long way round, didn't it — through Korea.

Through Korea first. Korean pop culture and Korean social media carried it. East Asian youth culture circles on its own loop now, and it bypasses the West entirely — which is exactly why you haven't read this anywhere in English.
So the culture's thawing from below while the politics freezes from above.
And nobody in the queue thinks of herself as diplomacy. She just wants dinner. That's what makes it durable.
[curious] Why this dish, though? Why now?

Because you build the bowl. You choose the ingredients, the noodle, the heat, the portion. It's photogenic, it feels controllable, almost healthy. The trend is less about China than about agency — indulgence you can audit. That it's Chinese is almost incidental.
[warmly] Does it last, though?

[drawn out] That's the open question. Japan had a bubble-tea boom in twenty-nineteen that ran from thirty-odd operators to sixty and then crashed — imports fell tenfold in a year. But malatang is a hot meal, not a sugary novelty, and it's riding a Chinese chain's supply network, not just a hashtag. It's already moving onto the convenience-store shelf. If it makes that leap, it's a fixture, not a fad.
When the Financial Times writes it up in three weeks…
…we already told you. That's the desk.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
